I would say what we can do: layered defences that lower the attack success rate, and design so that a successful attack has a small, bounded impact. I would propose a risk-based plan with measured attack success rates, least-privilege tools, approvals for risky actions, monitoring, and a tested incident process.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why not zero: probabilistic model behaviour, endless creative inputs, and adaptive attackers who keep searching. Detection classifiers can be bypassed with novel phrasing, so they reduce risk but are not a boundary. Real boundaries are deterministic: authorization, allow-lists, sandboxes, network egress rules, schema validation, and human approval.

Translate for the PM:

  • Define the worst plausible harm for this product and make that harm structurally impossible (for example, the assistant has no tool that can move money).
  • For the remainder, set acceptance thresholds: for example, under a certain ASR on the red-team suite per category, with over-refusal under a limit.
  • Ship with monitoring, kill switches and a response runbook.
  • Re-test on every change.

One-liners to keep: "Assume the model can be fooled; limit what a fooled model can do." "Output is untrusted input." "Measure over-refusal as well as attack success."

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Promising a guarantee, or promising "99% safe" with no definition.
  • Relying on a single detector.
  • Treating this as a launch checklist rather than ongoing work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you define an acceptable ASR? → By severity: near zero tolerance for critical harms, higher tolerance for low-severity ones, tied to compensating controls.
  2. Is a bigger model safer? → Often more robust to simple attacks, but also more capable when misused; it does not replace system design.
  3. What is deterministic here? → Permission checks, allow-lists, sandboxing, approvals.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "we will add filters". Senior: refuses the guarantee, defines bounded impact, metrics and process, and speaks the PM's language of risk acceptance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A launch review passed once the team replaced "the model won't do X" claims with "the system cannot do X" evidence.

questions.contextHtml: A consumer chatbot with 1.5 million daily users produces a response that tells a user how to combine two common chemicals dangerously. A screenshot goes viral: 2 million views in 4 hours; journalists contact the press office. Logs show a prompt update shipped 3 days earlier that loosened the tone ("be more casual, never lecture"). Moderation flagged nothing; the bot's safety evaluations ran on the old prompt only. On-call has no kill switch for individual capabilities; rolling back needs a full deploy taking 90 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through the incident and the review.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Patches the one prompt line and apologises. No containment strategy, no cause analysis of the process gap, no new controls.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many users saw similar outputs (log search by topic)? Which prompt versions are live? Do we have per-capability flags? Are regulators or app-store rules involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the prompt (or hotfix a restrictive system prefix); deploy an emergency output filter on hazardous-chemistry topics; enable more cautious mode; staff the incident channel; hold the communications plan with the press team.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The tone change reduced safety behaviour. (b) Moderation categories do not cover hazardous household chemistry. (c) No safety eval gate for prompt changes. Red herring: a jailbreak by the user; the query was plain.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the query across old and new prompt versions; run the red-team suite on the new prompt; search 3 days of logs for similar content.
  5. Root cause: Prompt changes were treated as copy edits and bypassed safety evaluation; a missing harm category and no fast kill switch extended exposure.
  6. Fix: Short term: rollback and filter. Long term: version prompts like code; CI gate running the safety and over-refusal suites on every prompt or model change; per-capability flags and a one-minute rollback; expand the harm taxonomy.
  7. Prevention: Blameless review with owners and dates; runbook for viral-harm incidents; drills; monitoring for topic spikes and user reports.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blame the engineer; I would not hide the issue. Be transparent with users and regulators as required, and avoid over-correcting into a refusal-heavy bot.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The model provider updated the model silently the same week. → Pin versions; run the suite on provider changes; keep a rollback model.
  • A user was harmed. → Escalate to legal; preserve evidence; follow notification obligations.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the fix that mattered was not the patch but the 60-second kill switch, which later contained a different incident within minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patch and apologise.
  • Hire: rollback, filter, search logs, add eval gate.
  • Strong hire: kill switches, communication plan, blameless review, taxonomy updates, drills, vendor-change controls.

questions.promptHtml: Design the safety and privacy architecture for an LLM assistant that handles patient messages for a clinic in the EU and the US.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Pulls everything together: compliance driving architecture, plus layered technical controls.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Start with data classification: patient messages are health data, so GDPR applies for EU patients and HIPAA for US ones. That drives architecture: a vendor with a signed BAA (Business Associate Agreement) and data-processing terms, zero-retention and regional endpoints, redaction and minimisation before the call, tenant and patient-level access control, no raw logging, human review for clinical content, and layered guardrails with tested incident response. Legal and compliance are involved from the first design review.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers:

  1. Governance: DPIA (data protection impact assessment), lawful basis and consent, vendor assessments, AI-regulation tiering (health is typically higher risk; verify with counsel), model cards.
  2. Data path: classify; minimise; redact or pseudonymise; route EU data to EU-region endpoints and US data to BAA-covered endpoints; private networking; customer-managed keys.
  3. Access control: patient-scoped retrieval with pre-filtering; staff roles; audit logs of who saw what.
  4. Model behaviour: the assistant triages and drafts; it does not diagnose. Grounded answers from approved clinical content with citations; abstention thresholds; emergency detection routes to human help and emergency numbers.
  5. Guardrails: input moderation, injection detection (patients may paste emails and documents), output PII/DLP scan, safe rendering, tool policy (can book appointments, cannot change prescriptions).
  6. Human oversight: clinician approval for anything clinical.
  7. Operations: redacted short-retention logs, deletion workflows across stores, red teaming focused on leakage and unsafe advice, bias testing across languages and dialects, kill switches and incident runbooks with breach-notification timelines (verify the exact windows with legal).
patient msg -> redact -> classify risk -> RAG (patient-scoped) -> LLM (regional, BAA)
           -> output DLP + groundedness + safety -> clinician review if clinical -> patient

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing the model first and compliance later.
  • Sending identifiable data to an endpoint without a BAA.
  • Treating the assistant as a clinician.
  • Logging full transcripts for debugging.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you test for leakage? → Planted canary patient records and cross-patient queries in CI and production.
  2. How do you handle a deletion request? → Fan-out across DB, vector index, caches, logs and training sets; verify with a synthetic user.
  3. Why human review? → Clinical harm is high-severity; the model can be wrong or fooled.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "redact PII and use a safe model". Senior: starts from regulation and data classes, builds region and vendor routing, structural isolation, scoped tools, clinician oversight, and operational readiness.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pilot stalled for months because the chosen provider had no BAA and no EU region; selecting vendors after the architecture would have avoided the rework.
